title: Mujaddara with bulgur
subtitle: Levantine bulgur and lentils with caramelised onion
excerpt: Mujaddara with bulgur is the coarser, more rustic version of the classic lentil and rice dish. Coarse bulgur gives a nuttier texture than rice, and the lentils become very soft, almost melting into the grain. Topped with a thick pile of dark caramelised onion, it is deeply filling and completely moreish.
sourceNotes: Mujaddara in its rice form (slug: mujaddara) is already published. This version uses coarse bulgur, which is a distinct regional variant common in parts of Lebanon and Syria. The two dishes have a meaningfully different texture and character.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water. The caramelised onion can be made a day ahead.

content.text: Mujaddara with bulgur is the dish that proves a very short ingredients list can produce something excellent. Lentils, coarse bulgur, onion, cumin, and olive oil. The technique is the cooking time: the onions must be cooked slowly for at least 20 minutes until they are deeply caramelised and almost jammy. They are what makes the dish.

The bulgur version has more texture than the rice version. The coarse grain gives each bite a slight chew, which works well against the soft lentils beneath. Served with a spoonful of cold yoghurt and a wedge of lemon, it is complete.
Use coarse bulgur (number 3 or 4 grind), not fine or medium. Fine bulgur will turn to mush in this dish.

Heat 4 tbsp of the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add all the sliced onions and cook slowly, stirring every few minutes, for 25 to 30 minutes until very dark golden and caramelised throughout. Remove half the onions and set aside for the topping.

Add the remaining olive oil to a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the remaining caramelised onion from the pan. Add the lentils, cumin, allspice, and salt. Pour in the water and bring to the boil. Reduce to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes until the lentils are almost tender. Stir in the bulgur, reduce to the lowest heat, cover tightly, and cook for 10 minutes until the bulgur has absorbed the liquid. Remove from the heat and leave covered for 5 minutes.
Fluff with a fork and taste for salt. Pile into a serving dish and top with the reserved caramelised onions. Serve with cold yoghurt and lemon wedges.

rows.cause: Lentils absorbed more water than expected before the bulgur was added
rows.fix: Add 100 ml of boiling water around the sides and continue covered for 5 more minutes.

rows.cause: Under-seasoned or cumin not toasted by the oil
rows.fix: Add the cumin to the oil before the lentils so it fries briefly; this blooms the spice. Adjust salt before serving.

rows.cause: Heat too high or stirred too often
rows.fix: Use medium heat only. Stir no more than every 5 minutes. Dark caramelised onions need time.

content.text: Serve with a simple tomato and cucumber salad alongside for freshness. A handful of toasted pine nuts scattered over the top adds texture. Some versions include a little chilli with the caramelised onion.

Mujaddara with bulgur keeps well and is often better the next day once the flavours have settled. Reheat gently with a splash of water and a drizzle of olive oil. Top with fresh caramelised onion when serving from fridge.

Mujaddara is eaten in many variations across a wide stretch of the Middle East. It is cheap, ancient, and deeply filling. The bulgur version is most common in Lebanon and Syria. It is the kind of dish that appears on tables every week in homes across the region.
